title: Joint and Marginal Distributions
short: A joint table gives P(X = x, Y = y); add across a row or down a column to get the marginal distributions.
trouble: Students read one cell of the joint table as a marginal probability.

blocks.html: Many questions involve two random variables at once: the number of heads and the number of tails, a customer's age group and spending. A two-way table, like those in conditional probability from two-way tables, holds their joint distribution, and the pmf of each variable alone sits in its margins.

The joint pmf is $p(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y)$; its cells are nonnegative and add to 1. The marginal pmfs come from adding across: $$p_X(x) = \sum_y p(x, y), \qquad p_Y(y) = \sum_x p(x, y).$$ Any event about $(X, Y)$ has probability equal to the sum of its cells.

The event $\{X = x\}$ splits into the disjoint pieces $\{X = x, Y = y\}$, one for each value $y$, so by the addition axiom $P(X = x)$ is the sum of that column. That is why these are called marginal: they were written in the margins of the table. The marginals do not determine the table, since many different tables have the same row and column totals; the joint pmf carries more information than the two marginals together.

blocks.q: From the table, find $P(X + Y \le 1)$ and $E[X]$.

blocks.html: A missing cell can be recovered from a margin: if you know $P(X = 2) = \frac{1}{3}$ and the cell $(2, 0)$ is 0, then the cell $(2, 1)$ must be $\frac{1}{3}$. Every row and every column adds to its marginal.

Reading one cell as a marginal: $P(X = 1, Y = 1) = \frac{1}{4}$ is not $P(X = 1)$, which also includes the cases with $Y = 0$. Check: a marginal must be at least as large as every cell in its row or column.
